## Anomaly
{"kind": "broken_link", "system": "tutorial", "title": "Tutorial steps stuck at 2 despite many events", "expected": "Within a round, tutorial_steps reaches 5 or more: claim (2), first cube (3), Dropper 2 buy (4), shop open (5), other upgrade (6, tutorial_done).", "observed": "Round 1 shows tutorial_steps=2 even though the plot was claimed, 103 cubes were collected, dropper_bought=2, shop_opened=1, and conveyor/speed upgrades were bought. tutorial_done never appears in the counters, so steps 3-6 apparently never advance or are never counted.", "severity": "high"}

## Investigation
Conclusion: {"root_cause": "TutorialService.notify only advances the strictly in-order ORDER chain: claimed, cashed, bought, shop, upgraded. A caller scan found notify('claimed') from TutorialService.setup and PlotClaimService, and notify('cashed') from CashInService. Nothing on the server ever calls notify with 'bought' or 'upgraded'. UpgradeService.purchase, where Dropper 2 and tier upgrades are bought, only bumps telemetry counters, fires remotes and calls CashInService.purchase, and never touches TutorialService. After 'cashed' (step 2) the chain waits for 'bought' forever. The client's 'shop' report is dropped as out of order, because notify ignores any event that is not the next unfired one. 'upgraded' is likewise never sent. So tutorial_steps stays at 2 and tutorial_done never happens, even though the purchases and shop opens themselves work. This conclusion comes from the code read plus the caller scan. The last probe did not return the counter values, so the stall at 2 was not confirmed live.", "file": "ServerScriptService/UpgradeService.luau", "evidence": "A grep probe over all ServerScriptService scripts for 'notify'/'TutorialService' found callers only in CashInService (\"cashed\"), PlotClaimService (\"claimed\"), Game (onPlotClaimed/start) and TutorialService itself. UpgradeService has no reference to TutorialService, and purchase() has no tutorial notification. TutorialService.notify returns early unless eventName equals the first unfired event in ORDER, and the client remo

Probe (Server): Find all callers of TutorialService.notify and the event names passed
```luau
local out={}

    if line:find('notify') or line:find('TutorialService') then table.insert(out,s.Name..':'..ln..': '..line:sub(1,140)) end
   end
  end
 end
end
return table.concat(out,'\n')
```

```luau
local RS=game:GetService('ReplicatedStorage')
local T=require(RS.ForgeTelemetry)
local keys={}
for k,v in pairs(T) do table.insert(keys,k..':'..type(v)) end
local snap=nil
for _,fn in ipairs({'snapshot','getAll','all','counters','dump'}) do
 local v=T[fn]
 if type(v)=='function' then local ok,r=pcall(v) if ok then snap=r break end elseif type(v)=='table' then snap=v break end
end
local sub=nil
if type(snap)=='table' then sub={} for k,v in pairs(snap) do if tostring(k):find('tutorial') or tostring(k):find('bought') or tostring(k):find('shop') then sub[k]=v end end end
return game:GetService('HttpService'):JSONEncode({keys=keys,sub=sub})
```

## Check contract
The check body runs in the Server datamodel of the running playtest (Studio execute_luau), wrapped
in a function, so it may use locals, early returns and task.wait (stay under 20 seconds in total).
It must return { ok = boolean, detail = string }. ok = true means the game behaves correctly.
A Luau error or a missing return counts as a failed run, but it does NOT prove the bug: only a clean
ok = false does. The playtest has the Studio player (Players:GetPlayers()[1]) once they have joined.
Live server modules can be reached with require(<ModuleScript>) or
game:GetService("ServerStorage").DevHook:Invoke(moduleName, method, ...).
Undo what the check sets up (cash, positions, spawned parts) before every return.
ok = false must mean "the game did the wrong thing". When the check cannot set up its situation (no player,
no plot, a part or module missing), call error("setup: <what is missing>") instead: that is a broken check,
not a proven bug, and an ok = false for it makes every fix look like a failure.
"Correct" is what the anomaly and the game's spec expect. Never redefine it just to get a failing check.
The third header line names the consumer: `-- consumer: <file>:<line>`, the game code (client or server)
that reads or uses what the check asserts, from the line-numbered code below. A check whose premise no game
code depends on proves nothing, and Forge will not count it.

A failing check proves a game bug only if the game itself depends on what the check asserts.
Name the consumer: the game code path (client or server) that reads or uses the asserted thing, as
<file>:<line> from the line-numbered code shown. A config value or the code that creates the thing is not a
consumer. If no game code reads it (the check expects an object in a place nothing looks, a name nothing
uses), the check's premise is wrong: it is a check bug, not a game bug.

## Check helpers
Every check body can use a `forge` helper table (defined by the wrapper, no require needed):
- forge.waitFor(fn, timeout) -> the first truthy value fn() returns within timeout seconds (default 10), else nil.
- forge.startRound(timeout) -> starts a round through the ForgeTest harness (no-op if workspace RoundState is
  already "Active") and waits until RoundState is "Active"; raises "setup: ..." when it cannot.
- forge.endRound() -> ends the round (call it before returning when the check started one).
A check never waits for a lobby countdown or a player to pick a mission: it calls forge.startRound().
